Q: How do I change a single index value in pandas dataframe? A: 
import pandas as pd

# Create DataFrame
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Name": ["John", "Alice", "Bob"],
    "Marks": [80, 90, 85]
})

# Change the value at index 1
df.at[1, "Marks"] = 95

print(df)

Output:

    Name  Marks
0   John     80
1  Alice     95
2    Bob     85

The .at[] method is used to update a single value in a Pandas DataFrame using its row index and column name. It is fast and efficient for modifying one specific cell. You can also use `.loc[]` if you need to update multiple rows or columns.

Q: Chaining multiple extraction operators >> inside while loop A:

Basically, the "expression"(a) file >> var1 >> var2 >> var3 will attempt to read three values from the file stream and place them into the specified variables. It's basically no different than cin >> myVar on it's own (except that it's chanining the input to multiple variables).

The value of that entire expression will be true if and only if all three values are read successfully.

In that case, the loop body will execute, the three values will be printed out, and the loop will go back to the top and try to get the next three values.

At the point where the expression evaluates as false (i.e., three values are not read), the loop will stop.

(a) The actual pathway from someStream >> someVariable to a Boolean value involves a few steps within the stream class (the return value from operator>> being converted to a Boolean with operator bool) but the above explanation should be good enough for most purposes.

Q: What is the equivalent Cmd.exe program for this PowerShell one-liner program? A:

Dissect the following PowerShell command:

Get-ChildItem -Path E:\input\ -Include *.xml | foreach { $html="E:\output\"+$_.basename+".html"; .\program $_.fullname $html}
  • Get-ChildItem -Path E:\input\ gets all the items under folder E:\input
  • -Include *.xml match the files with file name extension .xml
  • foreach { ... } applies the list to a loop, in each iteration the file object will be represented as $_
  • $html="E:\output\"+$_.basename+".html" for each found XML file, constructs a file path with .xml replaced by .html
  • .\program $_.fullname $html runs a program with 2 arguments: original .xml file path and the new .html file path

It is actually do-able in cmd.exe execept that it needs to loop / iterate directly on the folder, the rest can be achieved from there.

  • Use the for %%f in (PATH\PATTERN) do SOME_COMMAND syntax to loop over a given PATH and the files matching the PATTERN. Each matched item in the iteration is represented as %%f. Since you only want to scan for .xml files in E:\input folder, the command would be for %%f in (E:\input\*.xml) do SOME_COMMAND. The letter f is chosen arbitrarily, which stands for "file".
  • For SOME_COMMAND, we can simply use %%f to represent the original .xml file path. But to get the file path with an .html file name extension, we need to use the %%~nf.html syntax to get the base file name (%%~nf) with .html appended. Then we need to prepend E:\input\ to form the full path. So, it would be .\program %%f E:\input\%%~nf.html
  • There is a possibility that some file names could contain spaces. To cope with that, just quote the paths with a pair of double quotes " "
  • Add that to a .bat file. Need to add a @echo off to prevent it from showing the script file content.

The translated cmd.exe Batch script file (file name extension .bat) is like this:

@echo off

for %%f in (E:\input\*.xml) do .\program "%%f" "E:\input\%%~nf.html"

You can also use the for ... in (...) do (\n...\n) syntax to improve readability:

@echo off

for %%f in (E:\input\*.xml) do (
    .\program "%%f" "E:\input\%%~nf.html"
)

If you want to do the trick inside the cmd.exe window directly without using .bat file, remember to replace %% with %:

for %f in (E:\input\*.xml) do .\program "%f" "E:\input\%~nf.html"

See also: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/administration/windows-commands/for

Recursive version

If the original PowerShell command is changed to a recursive one, like so:

Get-ChildItem -Path E:\input\ -Recurse -Include *.xml | | foreach { $html="E:\output\"+$_.basename+".html"; .\program $_.fullname $html}

Then the equivalent cmd.exe counterpart can be achieved by using the /r option:

  • for /r [[<drive>:]<path>] recursively expands the search for all subfolders, as explained in the document.
  • Since the path is moved to the search, the rest of the for command should not include it, just use (PATTERN).

The recursive version of the cmd.exe command would become this one in a .bat file: (multi-line version)

@echo off 

for /r "E:\input\" %%f in (*.xml) do (
    .\program "%%f" "E:\input\%%~nf.html"
)

Single-line version (but @echo off is still there to suppress dumping of code):

@echo off 

for /r "E:\input\" %%f in (*.xml) do .\program "%%f" "E:\input\%%~nf.html"

And doing it directly in cmd.exe window: (%% -> %)

for /r "E:\input\" %f in (*.xml) do .\program "%f" "E:\input\%~nf.html"

Q: Best Way to Specify Linux Distribution Repo Version of Python Dependencies? A:

If you know it’s specific to RHEL, why not just build an RPM package using the Python macros for EPEL? The Fedora documentation, even though it’s aimed at Fedora packagers, explains those macros very well [1]. The macros basically expect a pyproject.toml. Then, you do the rpm build as part of your CI/CD:

rpkg srpm --outdir .
mock -r epel-10-x86_64 *.src.rpm
  1. https://docs.fedoraproject.org/en-US/packaging-guidelines/Python/
